# Introduction

The temperature dependence of biological rates is one of the most general regularities in
biology. Across taxa and levels of organisation, metabolic rates increase with temperature in
an approximately Boltzmann–Arrhenius fashion, and the fitted **activation energy** $E_a$ — the
slope of $\ln(\text{rate})$ against inverse temperature over the rising limb — clusters near a
"universal" value of ~0.6–0.7 eV [@gillooly2001; @delletal2011]. This apparent constancy
underpins metabolic scaling theory and is widely used to predict how biological processes
respond to warming. It also raises an unresolved mechanistic question: is an organism's $E_a$
set by a single rate-limiting enzyme whose temperature response the organism inherits, by an
aggregate over many enzymes, or by a shared thermodynamic constraint? The distinction matters,
because only a mechanistic account can explain the systematic *departures* from the universal
value that are also observed.

The most consequential such departure concerns methane. @yvondurocher2014 showed empirically
that the thermal sensitivity of methane flux is substantially higher than that of respiration
(and of photosynthesis), and — critically — that this ordering is **consistent from individual
methanogen cultures through microbial communities to whole ecosystems**. Cross-scale
consistency of an activation energy is a strong clue: it implies that the pattern is not an
emergent property of ecological aggregation but originates at the **cellular and enzymatic
scale** and propagates upward. What that cellular mechanism is, however, has remained unknown.
Why should the growth of a methanogen be more thermally sensitive than that of a respiring
bacterium — is it a more temperature-sensitive enzymatic machinery, or something about how that
machinery is organised and deployed?

Answering this requires a model in which the organism-level $E_a$ can be traced back to
individual enzymes. Enzyme- and temperature-constrained genome-scale models (etc-GEMs) provide
exactly this: they impose a temperature-dependent turnover on every enzyme and a shared
proteome budget, and predict the whole growth thermal performance curve (TPC) from
enzyme-constrained flux balance analysis. Building on a yeast thermal-etcGEM framework
[@Li2021], we construct etc-GEMs — to our knowledge the first for either taxon — of *E. coli*
(aerobic respiration, a complete electron transport chain) and *M. maripaludis* (hydrogenotrophic
methanogenesis, whose *only* energy-conserving pathway is the Wolfe-cycle backbone terminating
in the notoriously slow methyl-coenzyme-M reductase, Mcr). We calibrate each to a measured
growth TPC, quantify $E_a$ with a window-independent metric, and decompose it non-circularly
into a control-weighted aggregate of the per-enzyme activation energies plus named physiological
couplings. The answer, previewed here, is that the higher thermal sensitivity of methanogenesis
is **structural**: not a more temperature-sensitive enzyme set, but the concentration of growth
control on a single high-sensitivity energy backbone together with the absence of the
proteome-allocation buffer that dampens the respiring bacterium's $E_a$.

# Results

## Two etc-GEMs reproduce two separated activation energies {#sec-fig1}

Each etc-GEM was calibrated by Bayesian inference to its organism's measured growth TPC — *E.
coli* on rich Brain–Heart-Infusion broth over 7–46 °C [@vanderlinden2012], and *M. maripaludis*
on H2/CO2 defined medium over 15–52 °C [@jones1983]. Both reproduce their data: the
posterior-predictive median and 90% band pass through the observed points (@fig-scene, left and
centre), and the two curves differ visibly in the steepness of their rising limbs. Propagating
each calibration posterior through the Sharpe–Schoolfield fitter (Methods) yields the posterior
distribution of $E_a$ for each organism. These are **cleanly separated** — *M. maripaludis* at
~1.0 eV and *E. coli* at ~0.6 eV, with non-overlapping 90% credible intervals ([0.88, 1.16]
versus [0.60, 0.80]; @fig-scene, right). The empirical pattern of @yvondurocher2014 — higher
thermal sensitivity for methanogenesis than for respiration — is thus reproduced at the
cellular scale by two independent mechanistic models, and is robust to Bayesian parameter
uncertainty rather than an artefact of a point estimate. The remainder of the paper asks *why*.

![**Two organisms, two activation energies, reproduced mechanistically.** Calibrated (Bayesian) growth thermal performance curves for *E. coli* respiration (rich BHI) and *M. maripaludis* methanogenesis (H₂/CO₂): posterior-predictive median and 90% band with the observed data [@vanderlinden2012; @jones1983]. Right: the Sharpe–Schoolfield $E_a$ posteriors, propagated from the calibration draws, are separated (methanogen ~1.0 vs *E. coli* ~0.6 eV; dashed lines, observed values).](assets/fig1/fig1_scene_setter.png){#fig-scene fig-pos="H" width=100%}

## Both models predict the observed activation energy {#sec-valid}

Before decomposing the difference we establish that the modelled $E_a$ is a genuine prediction.
This test requires a stable metric, because the naive Boltzmann–Arrhenius slope is not one: the
rising limb is curved (enzyme kinetics are not log-linear in inverse temperature), so the fitted
slope depends on the arbitrary temperature window. Recomputed under five window conventions, the
slope $E_a$ of these very curves spans **0.42–1.41 eV per curve** — larger than the
cross-organism differences we seek to explain, and enough that under one window the two
organisms appear comparable while under another they are far apart (@tbl-window). We therefore
quantify $E_a$ throughout as the window-independent **Sharpe–Schoolfield $E$** [@schoolfield1981],
fit to the entire curve shape (Methods); the windowed slope is retained only as a deprecated
cross-check.

Under this metric the models agree with the data. The *E. coli* model gives $E_a = 0.68$ eV
against an observed 0.56 eV, sitting on the "universal" ~0.65 eV metabolic benchmark; the *M.
maripaludis* model gives 1.06 eV against an observed 1.04 (@tbl-comp). Because the per-enzyme
activation energies are model *inputs* (below), this agreement is a prediction of the
organism-level value, not a fitted output — and the methanogen genuinely sits ~1.6-fold above
the respiring bacterium.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-window
#| tbl-cap: "The naive Arrhenius-slope Ea is window-dependent, the Sharpe-Schoolfield E is not. Slope Ea (eV) for the model and observed curves under five window conventions (range shown), versus the window-independent Sharpe-Schoolfield E. The per-curve slope spread (0.42-1.41 eV) exceeds the cross-organism differences; the Sharpe-Schoolfield E is stable and makes model and observed agree."
#| output: asis
import pandas as pd
w = pd.read_csv("assets/tables/window_sensitivity.csv").set_index("curve")
ss = pd.read_csv("assets/tables/sharpe_schoolfield_fits.csv").set_index("curve")
cols = ["rel_10_95","full_below","rel_10_80","rel_30_90","rel_10_50"]
label = {"ecoli_tuned":"E. coli model","ecoli_observed_VdL":"E. coli observed",
         "methan_calibrated":"methanogen model","methan_observed_Jones":"methanogen observed"}
rows = []
for k,lab in label.items():
    r = w.loc[k, cols]
    rows.append({"curve":lab, "slope (10–95%)":round(float(w.loc[k,"rel_10_95"]),2),
                 "slope range":f"{r.min():.2f}–{r.max():.2f}",
                 "Sharpe–Schoolfield E":round(float(ss.loc[k,"SS_E_eV"]),2)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False))
```

## The difference is structural: control weighting and allocation, not enzyme thermodynamics {#sec-decomp}

To find what sets each $E_a$ we decompose it, by metabolic control analysis, into a
control-weighted aggregate of the per-enzyme activation energies and four named physiological
couplings (Methods, @eq-decomp). The framing is deliberately non-circular: the per-enzyme
activation energies $E_i$ are grounded model inputs, so we do not ask "what is $E_a$" but how
the organism-level value aggregates them and departs from their naive mean. @fig-decomp and
@tbl-comp give the result for both organisms on the same terms.

The central finding is counter-intuitive. The methanogen's enzymes are, on average, *less*
temperature-sensitive than the respiring bacterium's: the unweighted mean of the per-enzyme
activation energies is 0.51 eV in *M. maripaludis* versus 0.87 eV in *E. coli*. Intrinsic
enzyme thermodynamics alone would therefore predict the *opposite* ordering to the one observed.
The higher methanogen $E_a$ arises instead from how growth control is distributed and how the
proteome is allocated.

First, growth control concentrates on the high-$E_a$ methanogenesis backbone. In a
hydrogenotroph, energy metabolism *is* growth: essentially all catabolism flows through the
Wolfe cycle, so a small set of energy enzymes — formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase (Fwd), the
methyltransferase (Mtr), Mcr, the methylene-tetrahydromethanopterin reductase (Mer), the
heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr) and the hydrogenases — carries **89% of the control term**, and
these enzymes are themselves high-$E_a$ (mean 0.77 eV against a proteome mean of 0.51). This
concentration lifts the effective enzyme activation energy by **+0.34 eV**. In *E. coli*, by
contrast, growth control is spread across a broad biosynthetic proteome, and the analogous
control-weighting term adds only **+0.11 eV**.

Second, the methanogen lacks the proteome-allocation buffer that lowers *E. coli*'s $E_a$. In
*E. coli*, the Scott-type growth law reallocates proteome toward ribosomes as growth accelerates,
which shrinks the metabolic sector at higher temperature and pulls the organism $E_a$ down by
**−0.13 eV**. *M. maripaludis*, which maintains a **constant ribosomal proteome fraction** and
full methanogenesis capacity across growth rate [@muller2021], applies no such buffer: its
allocation term, measured on its own sectored model, is **+0.00 eV**. Both allocation terms are
therefore grounded in each organism's own measured allocation strategy, making the comparison
symmetric rather than an artefact of model structure.

Together these two structural terms — the control-weighting difference (+0.24 eV) and the
allocation asymmetry (+0.13 eV) — account for essentially the entire +0.38 eV gap in organism
$E_a$. The two remaining terms nearly cancel: the methanogen's lower average enzyme activation
energy (−0.36 eV) is offset by a larger **aggregation** term (+0.39 eV), the tendency of its
narrow, synchronised control on a few backbone enzymes to steepen the composite growth curve
where *E. coli*'s broad control flattens it. We note that although the aggregation term is the
largest single contribution, it is also the most sensitive to the details of the metric; the
robust conclusion — that the difference is set by control weighting and allocation — does not
depend on it.

![**What moves the organism $E_a$ away from the naive enzyme mean.** Signed contribution of each named term (Sharpe–Schoolfield $E$; both organisms carrying a proteome-sector layer), sign-coloured. The higher methanogen $E_a$ is driven by control weighting (+0.11 vs +0.34 eV) and the allocation asymmetry (−0.13 vs +0.00 eV), not by higher intrinsic enzyme temperature-sensitivity (naive mean 0.87 vs 0.51 eV).](assets/figures/cross_organism_signed_contributions.png){#fig-decomp fig-pos="H" width=100%}

```{python}

#| tbl-cap: "Symmetric cross-organism decomposition of the Sharpe-Schoolfield activation energy. Both organisms carry a proteome-sector/growth-law layer, so the allocation term is measured for each (E. coli Scott growth law; M. maripaludis constant-ribosome flat law). The +0.38 eV difference is set by control-weighting and allocation, not by a higher intrinsic enzyme Ea (naive mean 0.87 vs 0.51). Both models match the observed SS-E."

import pandas as pd
```

## The ordering is robust to the uncertain Mcr turnover {#sec-mcr}

The turnover number of the terminal methanogenesis enzyme, Mcr, is uncertain for a mesophile —
the literature spans roughly 3–294 s⁻¹. Because Mcr is a candidate rate-controller, we swept its
$k_\text{cat}$ across this range and repeated the analysis (@tbl-mcr). The organism $E_a$ remains
between 1.01 and 1.27 eV throughout, always well above the *E. coli* value of 0.68, and the
methanogenesis backbone carries 83–103% of the control term across the whole range. The ordering
and the backbone-control finding are therefore robust to this uncertainty. What does change is
the identity of the single leading enzyme: Mcr dominates when it is slow (a low turnover makes it
expensive in enzyme mass and thus high in control), Fwd leads when Mcr is fast, and the two
co-lead at the calibrated value. The classic expectation that Mcr specifically sets the
methanogen $E_a$ therefore holds only when Mcr is slow; the robust statement is that the *energy
backbone as a whole*, not any single enzyme, carries the high thermal sensitivity.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mcr
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity to the Mcr turnover number (3-294/s). The organism SS-E stays well above E. coli's 0.68 and the backbone fraction of the control term stays near-total across the range; only the leading enzyme shifts (Mcr when slow, Fwd when fast)."
#| output: asis
import pandas as pd
m = pd.read_csv("assets/tables/mcr_sweep.csv")[["Mcr_kcat","SS_E","backbone_frac_of_control","top3"]]
m.columns = ["Mcr kcat (1/s)","organism SS-E (eV)","backbone fraction of control","leading enzymes"]
print(m.to_markdown(index=False))
```

# Discussion

The higher thermal sensitivity of methanogenesis relative to respiration [@yvondurocher2014] has
a concrete cellular mechanism, and it is not the intuitive one. The methanogen's enzymes are not
individually more temperature-sensitive — on average they are less so. Instead the organism-level
activation energy is a **control-weighted, allocation-modulated aggregate** of the per-enzyme
activation energies, and two structural features of methanogenic physiology raise it. Because a
hydrogenotroph conserves energy through a single narrow pathway, growth control concentrates
almost entirely on that high-activation-energy energy backbone, rather than being diluted across
a broad biosynthetic proteome as in a respiring heterotroph. And because *M. maripaludis*
maintains a constant ribosomal fraction and full methanogenesis capacity across growth rate
[@muller2021], it lacks the growth-law proteome reallocation that buffers *E. coli*'s activation
energy downward. Each term is grounded in the organism's own measured allocation strategy, so the
comparison reflects biology rather than a modelling choice.

This reframes the "universal" metabolic activation energy. Its approximate constancy need not
imply a conserved enzyme or a fixed biophysical constant; the same control-weighted-aggregation
mechanism, acting on a **different controlling set** and modulated by a **different allocation
strategy**, produces systematically different organism-level values. A respiring bacterium lands
near the benchmark because its control is broad and allocation-buffered; a methanogen sits well
above it because its control is narrow and unbuffered. The corollary is a link, to our knowledge
not previously drawn, between **proteome-allocation strategy and thermal sensitivity**: how an
organism partitions and couples its proteome is a determinant of how steeply its growth responds
to temperature. This connection is significant precisely because of the cross-scale consistency
that motivated the question — if the cellular mechanism is control concentration on a
high-$E_a$, unbuffered energy pathway, then that mechanism is what propagates the methanogenesis
signal from cultures up to the ecosystem fluxes of @yvondurocher2014.

Several caveats bound these conclusions. The aggregation term, though the largest single
contribution to the cross-organism difference, is the most sensitive to the definition of the
activation-energy metric; we have therefore rested the mechanistic conclusion on the
control-weighting and allocation terms, which alone account for the observed gap. The mesophilic
turnover of Mcr is the dominant single-parameter uncertainty: the ordering and the
backbone-control result are robust across its plausible range, but the identity of the single
most rate-controlling enzyme is not, and a direct measurement of mesophilic Mcr $k_\text{cat}$
would sharpen the attribution. The per-enzyme activation energies are grounded inputs (from
macromolecular rate theory, sequence-based optima, a melting proteome, and — for the methanogen —
a deep-learning turnover predictor corrected against literature kinetics), so the result is an
attribution given those inputs rather than an ab-initio prediction of the numerical value.
Finally, this is a two-organism comparison; the mechanism is a hypothesis that a broader survey
should test.

The natural next test is the third process in the @yvondurocher2014 ordering. Photosynthesis has
an even lower thermal sensitivity than respiration, and a cyanobacterial etc-GEM — with its
light-driven energy metabolism and distinct proteome economy — would provide a demanding,
directional test of whether the control-and-allocation framework generalises across all three
metabolic strategies. If it does, a phenomenological "universal" activation energy will have been
replaced by a mechanistic, organism-specific, and predictive account of thermal sensitivity.

# Methods

We represent each organism by the same layered enzyme- and temperature-constrained
genome-scale model (etc-GEM), and write out the full constraint system below before describing
where the two taxa depart. The thermal core follows the yeast etc-GEM of @Li2021; we take from
existing work the GECKO/sMOMENT enzyme constraint [@Sanchez2017; @Domenzain2022], macromolecular
rate theory [@Hobbs2013], and the proteome-sector growth law [@Basan2015; @Scott2010], and add:
application to two new taxa; measured- and machine-learning-grounded per-enzyme parameters; an
**organism-specific** allocation law; an exact-likelihood Bayesian calibration (rather than
approximate Bayesian computation); the window-independent Sharpe–Schoolfield activation energy;
and the mechanistic, control-weighted $E_a$ decomposition. Energies are in J mol⁻¹, entropies
and heat capacities in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, temperatures in kelvin, $R=8.314$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; the written
equations mirror the implementation (`enzyme_cost.py`, `mmrt.py`, `unfolding.py`, `sectors.py`,
`sharpe_schoolfield.py`, `ea_dissection.py`).

## The etc-GEM framework {#sec-methods-fw}

**Enzyme-constrained flux balance.** Growth is the biomass flux $v_\text{bio}$ found by linear
programming under mass balance and enzyme capacity. At steady state
$$\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0},$$ {#eq-fba}
where $\mathbf{S}$ is the stoichiometric matrix and $\mathbf{v}$ the flux vector
(mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹) with lower/upper bounds encoding reversibility and medium availability. Each
reaction is limited by the amount of catalytically competent (native) enzyme,
$$0\le v_i \le k_{\text{cat},i}(T)\,f_{N,i}(T)\,[E]_i,$$ {#eq-cap}
with turnover $k_{\text{cat},i}(T)$ (@eq-kcat), total enzyme $[E]_i$, and native fraction
$f_{N,i}(T)\in[0,1]$ (@eq-fn) — only folded protein catalyses, while denatured protein still
occupies the budget. Rather than an enzyme variable per reaction, we impose the equivalent
**sMOMENT** total-protein-pool form: a shared, sector-partitioned budget bounds the summed
per-flux enzyme demand (@eq-pool).

**Temperature-dependent turnover.** Each enzyme's turnover follows transition-state (Eyring)
theory with a macromolecular-rate-theory heat-capacity term [@Hobbs2013],
$$k_{\text{cat},i}(T)=\frac{k_B T}{h}\exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{\Delta G^{\ddagger}_i(T)}{RT}\Big),\;
\Delta G^{\ddagger}_i(T)=\Delta H^{\ddagger}_i+\Delta C^{\ddagger}_{p,i}(T-T_0)
-T\big(\Delta S^{\ddagger}_i+\Delta C^{\ddagger}_{p,i}\ln(T/T_0)\big),$$ {#eq-kcat}
with Boltzmann and Planck constants $k_B,h$, reference $T_0$, and per-enzyme activation
enthalpy, entropy and heat capacity $\Delta H^{\ddagger}_i,\Delta S^{\ddagger}_i,
\Delta C^{\ddagger}_{p,i}$. A negative $\Delta C^{\ddagger}_p$ makes $\ln k_\text{cat}$
single-peaked, so the **rising-limb activation energy emerges from @eq-kcat** rather than being
imposed. Turnover is carried relative to its value at each enzyme's optimum $T_{\text{opt},i}$,
$\widehat{k}_i(T)=k_{\text{cat},i}(T)/k_{\text{cat},i}(T_{\text{opt},i})$, with
$\Delta H^{\ddagger}_i$ fixed by the peak condition $\mathrm d\ln k_\text{cat}/\mathrm dT=0$ at
$T_{\text{opt},i}$.

**Two-state unfolding and the effective cost.** The high-temperature collapse is set by
denaturation: a native$\leftrightarrow$unfolded equilibrium keyed on the melting temperature
$T_{m,i}$,
$$f_{N,i}(T)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\!\big(-\Delta G_{u,i}(T)/RT\big)},\;
\Delta G_{u,i}(T)=\Delta H_{TH,i}+\Delta C_{p,u,i}(T-T_H)-T\Delta S_{TS,i}-T\Delta C_{p,u,i}\ln(T/T_S),$$ {#eq-fn}
with universal convergence temperatures $T_H=373.5$ K, $T_S=385$ K, and unfolding parameters
solved from $T_{m,i}$ (with $T_{90}$ or protein length) via $\Delta G_{u,i}(T_{m,i})=0$ and
$\Delta G_{u,i}(T_{90})=-RT_{90}\ln 9$. Combining anchored turnover and native fraction, the
per-flux enzyme cost is
$$c_i(T)=\frac{\text{base}_i}{\widehat{k}_i(T)\,f_{N,i}(T)\,\lambda_k},\qquad
\text{base}_i=\frac{\text{MW}_i}{k_{\text{cat},i}(T_{\text{opt},i})\cdot 3600},$$ {#eq-cost}
with enzyme mass $\text{MW}_i$ (kDa $=$ g mmol⁻¹), the factor 3600 converting s⁻¹ to h⁻¹, and a
global turnover-level multiplier $\lambda_k$ (`kcat_scale`, nominal 1). Denatured enzyme still
occupies the budget but does not catalyse, so cost is inflated by $1/f_{N,i}$ — the origin of the
falling limb, keyed on stability $T_m$ and thus decoupled from the rising-limb $E_a$.

**Proteome sectors, the pool budget, and the growth law.** The total modelled protein
$P_\text{tot}$ is split into coarse sectors [@Basan2015; @Scott2010] summing to one — metabolic
$f_\text{metab}$, biosynthesis/ribosomal $f_\text{bio}$, and maintenance $f_\text{maint}$ — and
growth maximises $v_\text{bio}$ under a metabolic-pool bound and a biosynthesis (translation)
cap,
$$\sum_i c_i(T)\,(v_i^{+}+v_i^{-})\le f_\text{metab}\,P_\text{tot},\qquad
\kappa\,v_\text{bio}\le f_\text{bio}\,P_\text{tot},$$ {#eq-pool}
where $v_i^{\pm}\ge 0$ are forward/reverse fluxes and $\kappa$ (`translation_coeff`) is the
ribosomal demand per unit biomass flux, auto-calibrated once at build so the two caps co-limit
at the nominal split (enabling sectors does not move nominal growth). The metabolic budget is
grounded independently,
$$P_\text{metab}=f_\text{metab}\,P_\text{tot},\qquad P_\text{tot}=\sigma\,P^{\text{lit}},$$ {#eq-alloc}
with in-vivo saturation $\sigma$ and literature total protein $P^{\text{lit}}$. Optionally the
sectors follow a proteome-conserving growth law in which the ribosomal and metabolic fractions
move with growth rate at a common slope $s$, $f_\text{bio}(\mu)=f_{\text{bio},0}+s\mu$ and
$f_\text{metab}(\mu)=f_{\text{metab},0}-s\mu$ ($\mu=v_\text{bio}$), keeping both caps linear,
$$(\kappa-sP_\text{tot})\,v_\text{bio}\le f_{\text{bio},0}P_\text{tot},\qquad
\sum_i c_i(T)(v_i^{+}+v_i^{-})+sP_\text{tot}\,v_\text{bio}\le f_{\text{metab},0}P_\text{tot}.$$ {#eq-growthlaw}
The slope $s$ is the scientifically load-bearing organism-specific quantity: it is set from each
organism's own proteome data (below), and its value is the origin of the allocation term in the
$E_a$ decomposition.

**Maintenance.** A temperature-dependent non-growth maintenance ATP demand rises with
temperature [@Madkaikar2023],
$$\text{NGAM}(T)=a_\text{m}\Big(1-b\exp\!\big[\tfrac{-E_m}{k_B}\big(\tfrac1{T_\text{ref}}-\tfrac1T\big)\big]\Big),\quad\text{floored at }T_\text{ref},$$ {#eq-ngam}
with amplitude $a_\text{m}$, $b\approx0.62$, apparent activation energy $E_m\approx0.5$ eV,
$T_\text{ref}=298.15$ K and $k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV K⁻¹, imposed as
$v_\text{ATPM}\ge\text{NGAM}(T)\,f_\text{maint}/f_\text{maint}^{\text{nom}}$; the growth-associated
maintenance (GAM) is the ATP demand carried in the biomass reaction. At each grid temperature FBA
maximises $\mu(T)=\max_{\mathbf v}v_\text{bio}$ subject to @eq-fba, @eq-pool and the maintenance
floor, tracing the organismal TPC.

**The activation energy.** From $\mu(T)$ we read standard descriptors — the optimum
$T_\text{opt}=\arg\max_T\mu$, the maximum rate $r_\text{max}$, the critical limits
$CT_\text{min}/CT_\text{max}$ (where $\mu$ falls to 5% of $r_\text{max}$), and the niche width.
The naive Boltzmann–Arrhenius activation energy — the slope of $\ln\mu$ against $-1/(k_BT)$ over
a rising-limb window — is window-dependent (Results, @sec-valid), so we report instead the
**window-independent Sharpe–Schoolfield $E$** [@schoolfield1981], the rising-limb activation
energy of the high-temperature-inactivation model
$$\mu(T)=r_{T_\text{ref}}\,\frac{\exp[(E/k_B)(1/T_\text{ref}-1/T)]}{1+\exp[(E_h/k_B)(1/T_h-1/T)]},$$ {#eq-ssf}
fit to the whole calibrated curve by nonlinear least squares at a fixed $T_\text{ref}=20$ °C,
where $E$ is the reported $E_a$ and $E_h,T_h$ describe the high-$T$ deactivation. The same fit is
applied identically to model and observed curves and to both organisms.

**Bayesian calibration.** Each model is calibrated to one measured growth TPC with a
gradient-free ensemble sampler (emcee), warm-started at the posterior mode and run to an
autocorrelation-based stop. The deterministic simulator $\theta\mapsto\mu(T)$ is combined with a
Gaussian discrepancy likelihood
$$\ln L(\theta)=-\tfrac12\sum_t\Big[\frac{(\mu^{\text{obs}}_t-\mu(T_t;\theta))^2}{\text{sd}_t^2+\sigma_\text{disc}^2}+\ln\big(2\pi(\text{sd}_t^2+\sigma_\text{disc}^2)\big)\Big],$$ {#eq-lik}
with per-point measurement SD $\text{sd}_t$ (zero where none is reported) and a free
model-discrepancy scale $\sigma_\text{disc}$. Only a small set of **global scalars** is freed —
$\{\lambda_k$ (`kcat_scale`), $\sigma$, $dT_\text{opt}$, `topt_scale`, `dCp_scale`, $dT_m$,
`tm_scale`, $f_\text{metab}$, $f_\text{maint}$, `ngam_scale`, `ngam_steepness`,
$\sigma_\text{disc}\}$ — each transforming the *whole* grounded per-enzyme distribution while
preserving its shape (a uniform shift, stretch or rescale), never a per-enzyme free parameter.
Positive-only parameters are sampled in log space; priors are provenance-based (measured sector
fractions tight; the in-vivo saturation a broad Normal on 0.45; magnitude and envelope levers
LogNormal about their nominal). The emergent (nothing-fit) model and the calibrated posterior are
kept distinct throughout.

**The control-weighted activation-energy decomposition.** To ask what sets each $E_a$ we
decompose the Sharpe–Schoolfield $E$, by metabolic control analysis, into a control-weighted mean
of the per-enzyme rising-limb activation energies and four named couplings relative to the naive
(unweighted) enzyme mean:
$$E_a^\text{org}=\overline{E_i}+\underbrace{\big(\textstyle\sum_i\hat C_iE_i-\overline{E_i}\big)}_{\text{control weighting}}+\Delta_\text{alloc}+\Delta_\text{maint}+\Delta_\text{agg}.$$ {#eq-decomp}
The construction is non-circular: the per-enzyme $E_i$ — the rising-limb Arrhenius activation
energy of each enzyme's turnover $k_{\text{cat},i}(T)$ alone (the folding term is the high-$T$
deactivation, contributing a negligible $-0.008$ eV control-weighted) — are model *inputs*, and
the result is how the organism value aggregates and departs from them. The growth flux-control
coefficients $\hat C_i=\partial\ln\mu/\partial\ln k_{\text{cat},i}$ are computed by symmetric
perturbation and re-solve and normalised over the controlling set. The **allocation** term is
isolated by disabling the growth-law coupling (@eq-growthlaw), the **maintenance** term by
flattening NGAM($T$), and the **aggregation** term is computed directly as the Sharpe–Schoolfield
$E$ of the kinetic-backbone aggregate curve minus the control-weighted per-enzyme mean. Both
organisms are analysed on the calibrated model at their operating point, each carrying its own
sector/growth-law layer, with the uncosted energy side-reactions closed. For Figure 1 the saved
calibration draws were propagated through @eq-ssf to obtain the $E_a$ posteriors.

## Taxon-specific construction and departures {#sec-methods-departures}

The two models instantiate the same framework but differ, layer by layer, in ways that are
either technical (base reconstruction, parameter provenance) or scientifically load-bearing (the
allocation law). @tbl-departures summarises the contrasts; the two most consequential are the
kcat provenance for the energy core and — the term that carries part of the $E_a$ difference —
the allocation law.

**Base network and enzyme layer.** *E. coli* starts from iML1515 [@Monk2017] as a pre-built GECKO
ecModel (eciML1515) [@Sanchez2017; @Domenzain2022] carrying reference turnovers and masses for
2,560 enzymes; *M. maripaludis* starts from the plain iMR539 reconstruction [@richards2016], onto
which we build the sMOMENT enzyme layer here (527 enzymatic reactions mapped to UniProt masses).

**Curation.** *E. coli* required closing four uncosted O₂-sink reactions (two quinol
monooxygenases, a malate:O₂ oxidoreductase, a cuprous oxidase) that form a futile O₂ cycle. *M.
maripaludis* required a carbon-honest autotroph curation: folding the dispensable archaellum
glycoprotein out of biomass, repairing a selenocysteinyl-tRNA recycling gap, closing organic-
carbon leaks and freeing the pinned methane exchange, and supplying two non-synthesisable vitamin
cofactors as trace supplements.

**Turnover provenance.** *E. coli* uses the GECKO built-in $k_\text{cat}$ refined by DLTKcat
[@Qiu2024]. For *M. maripaludis* the energy-conserving core was set from measured specific
activities (the electron-bifurcation hydrogenase/heterodisulfide-reductase complexes [@milton2018],
converted to $k_\text{cat}$ via complex masses), the biosynthetic bulk from DLTKcat corrected for a
systematic archaeal underprediction (28% of predictions below 1 s⁻¹) with cited literature/BRENDA
overrides for the highest-cost offenders and a documented 1 s⁻¹ floor, and a mean fallback; Mcr —
the $E_a$ target — was sourced explicitly ($k_\text{cat}\approx59$ s⁻¹, 3–294 s⁻¹ range, swept in
@sec-mcr).

**Optima and stability.** *E. coli* $T_{\text{opt},i}$ and $T_{m,i}$ are grounded per enzyme
(sequence-based optimum predictor [@LiEngqvist2019]; measured melting proteome [@Leuenberger2017])
for ~90% of enzymes. For *M. maripaludis* these predictors were not run; both use a documented
mesophile prior (a flagged limitation refined by M4's $dT_\text{opt}$/$dT_m$).

**The allocation law (load-bearing departure).** *E. coli* uses the bacterial Scott growth law
[@Scott2010]: the ribosomal fraction *rises* with growth rate (slope $s\approx0.33$), which
shrinks the metabolic sector at higher temperature and buffers $E_a$ downward. *M. maripaludis*
holds a **constant** ribosomal fraction across growth rate [@muller2021] — a documented
alternative allocation strategy — so its slope $s=0$ (a flat law), and the allocation buffer
vanishes. This physiological difference, not a modelling choice, is one of the two terms that
explain the $E_a$ difference (Results, @sec-decomp).

**Maintenance, medium and saturation.** Maintenance NGAM($T$) uses an *E. coli* amplitude for the
bacterium and the **measured** *M. maripaludis* maintenance energy [@goyal2015] for the methanogen.
Validation/calibration is against BHI-rich growth (Van Derlinden 2012 [@vanderlinden2012]) for *E.
coli* and H₂/CO₂ growth (Jones 1983 [@jones1983]) for the methanogen. Both take the in-vivo
saturation $\sigma$ from the same literature range [@Davidi2016; @Heckmann2020]. Full per-model
construction, parameter and provenance tables, and robustness analyses are in the Supplement.

| Layer | *E. coli* (respiration) | *M. maripaludis* (methanogenesis) |
|---|---|---|
| Base GEM | iML1515 [@Monk2017] → GECKO eciML1515 | iMR539 [@richards2016] → our sMOMENT layer |
| Curation | 4 uncosted O₂ sinks closed | carbon-honest autotroph (archaellin/SeCys/leaks) |
| $k_\text{cat}$ | ecModel built-in + DLTKcat | measured core [@milton2018] + DLTKcat + overrides + floor |
| $T_\text{opt}/T_m$ | sequence/meltome-grounded (~90%) | mesophile prior |
| **Allocation law** | **Scott: ribosome fraction rises with $\mu$ ($s\!\approx\!0.33$)** | **Müller: constant ribosome fraction ($s=0$)** |
| Maintenance | *E. coli* NGAM($T$) | measured NGAM [@goyal2015] |
| Medium / curve | BHI rich, Van Derlinden 2012 | H₂/CO₂, Jones 1983 |
| Saturation $\sigma$ | 0.45 (0.4–0.5) [@Davidi2016; @Heckmann2020] | 0.45 (0.4–0.5) [@Davidi2016; @Heckmann2020] |

: Where the two etc-GEMs depart, by model layer. The allocation-law row (Scott rising vs Müller constant ribosome fraction) is the scientifically load-bearing difference. {#tbl-departures}

# Data and code availability

All figures and tables are generated from the analysis outputs of the two etc-GEMs and their
cross-organism comparison. The complete model construction for both organisms, the parameter and
data-source tables, the window-sensitivity audit, the calibration diagnostics, and the robustness
analyses are provided in the Supplement.
